1.pericope_label: The same day went Jesus out of the house, and sat by the sea side. And great multitudes were gathered together unto him, so that he went into a ship, and sat; and the whole multitude stood on the shore. And he spake many things unto them in parables, saying, Behold, a sower went forth to sow; And when he sowed, some seeds fell by the way side, and the fowls came and devoured them up: Some fell upon stony places, where they had not much earth: and forthwith they sprung up, because they had no deepness of earth: And when the sun was up, they were scorched; and because they had no root, they withered away. And some fell among thorns; and the thorns sprung up, and choked them: But other fell into good ground, and brought forth fruit, some an hundredfold, some sixtyfold, some thirtyfold. Who hath ears to hear, let him hear.

schools.summary: Robertson allows the plain sixth day but thinks a week likelier, takes the word parable from placing alongside for measurement, and separates it from the fable, which puts things as they are not in nature, and from the self-explaining allegory, warning that a parable usually carries one main point and that much heresy has come of pressing details. Ellicott insists on Eastern tillage against English assumptions: ground less perfectly cleared, a road crossing the field, rock under an inch of soil, so that the wayside is the skirt of the path, the stony place a thin stratum over rock where growth is rapid through the very circumstance that kills, and the thorns invisible at sowing, their roots left below, the ears slowly strangled in a survival not of the fittest but of the strongest; on the yield he notes the article, the good ground, and calls the hundredfold uncommon but attested. Barnes gives four purposes for parables at once, to make truth interesting, to reach ignorant hearers through the senses, to drive a rebuke home as Nathan did to David, and to hide from one part of an audience what another was meant to grasp; he adds that the headland was what the plough had not touched, that seed on rock sprang sooner only because it had less earth to come through, and refuses the arithmetic of the yield, since a parable teaches a general truth. Lightfoot supplies the rabbinic background, that no figure was more familiar and that their religion might itself be called parabolical, folded up in ceremonies.

Gill dates the withdrawal to the day of the dumb devil and the answer to the Pharisees, and places the house at Capernaum, left because it would not hold the people. Calvin reads the parable against his own century as much as the first, that if men who ran from far off like hungry persons are called barren soil we need not wonder the Gospel bears no fruit in many now.

Clarke derives the word from casting one thing beside another, spiritual things compared with natural, and takes the hundredfold as literal and marvellous, reporting his own sowing of oats at Millbrook and a divided wheat plant at Cambridge that gave twenty-one thousand ears; he also thinks the vessel was kept on the lake for our Lord's use. Wesley agrees about the vessel, notes that the hindrances are named in the order they arrive, and insists that it is not God's will that stops the seed but the hearers' own perverseness.

Henry observes that Christ preached at both ends of the day, that no Pharisees were present so that he had better their room than their company, and that his pulpit was a ship, not made for the purpose as Ezra's was but converted to the use for want of a better.

Chrysostom lays the loss on the soil and not the sower, observes that with minds, unlike earth, rock may be made rich ground and thorns rooted out, notes that the careless are not named openly lest they be alienated, and that the Lord did not desist from sowing though he foresaw the waste.
Augustine takes the same day to mean either that these things followed at once or that little intervened.

debates.question: Why did Christ teach in parables?

positions.position: To make truth interesting, to reach the ignorant through the senses, to drive home a rebuke, and to hide from some what others were to grasp
To place an illustration alongside the truth, usually carrying one main point
Following a form of rhetoric already familiar among the Jews

debates.question: How is the hundredfold to be taken?

positions.position: Literally and marvellously, as agricultural experiment confirms
Uncommon but attested, the article marking the good ground
Not to be pressed, since a parable teaches a general truth

outliers.claim: Supports the hundredfold from his own field trials, an oat grain returning a hundred and nineteen and a divided wheat plant yielding twenty-one thousand ears

10.pericope_label: And the disciples came, and said unto him, Why speakest thou unto them in parables? He answered and said unto them, Because it is given unto you to know the mysteries of the kingdom of heaven, but to them it is not given. For whosoever hath, to him shall be given, and he shall have more abundance: but whosoever hath not, from him shall be taken away even that he hath. Therefore speak I to them in parables: because they seeing see not; and hearing they hear not, neither do they understand. And in them is fulfilled the prophecy of Esaias, which saith, By hearing ye shall hear, and shall not understand; and seeing ye shall see, and shall not perceive: For this people’s heart is waxed gross, and their ears are dull of hearing, and their eyes they have closed; lest at any time they should see with their eyes, and hear with their ears, and should understand with their heart, and should be converted, and I should heal them. But blessed are your eyes, for they see: and your ears, for they hear. For verily I say unto you, That many prophets and righteous men have desired to see those things which ye see, and have not seen them; and to hear those things which ye hear, and have not heard them.

schools.summary: Ellicott places the disciples in the boat, asks why parables now and why to plain peasants rather than men trained in the rabbinic schools, and defines a mystery against the dictionary sense of something awfully obscure as a secret kept from others and revealed to the initiated; he grants that Mark and Luke make the purpose penal and that this is the sense here, yet finds mercy under it, since a parable roused none of the enmity plain speech had roused and might set a man thinking. Barnes holds that mystery means a thing concealed rather than a thing incomprehensible, naming as examples that the gospel was for the Gentiles and that the Messiah must die, and judges it just that opportunities long misimproved be withdrawn. Robertson traces the word to the initiate and behind him to the closing of the mouth, notes the eastern mystery religions, and observes that Paul uses it of what was hidden and is now made known. Lightfoot dates the stupor of the nation long before the passion, laid on it by Pharisaism and the sottishness of tradition, and sends the reader to Romans, where Paul repeats these words.

Calvin holds that Christ deliberately spoke so as to be a riddle; the word is bright in its own nature and dark only as the world darkens it, yet the Lord keeps his secrets from the reprobate, and to call the apostles' privilege given excludes all merit. He refuses the reading of improvement in the proverb of having, taking it instead of God not forsaking the work of his own hands, while the reprobate, whose gifts have glitter but no root, waste away in their own poverty. Gill notes that more than the twelve were present and applies the promise inward, that true grace grows and the Spirit leads into all truth.

Clarke widens the mysteries to the prophetic account of the Church folded into the parables that follow, given first to a few because those few would publish it, hears in the proverb of having an everyday saying that presents are made to the rich, and guards the prophets from the inference, since they were not shut out from salvation, only their time was not yet. Wesley makes the proverb turn on improvement and calls it the grand rule of God's dealing with men, fixed as the pillars of heaven.

Chrysostom admires the disciples' timing and charity, that they did not ask before the multitude and asked not why speakest thou to us but to them; he denies that the saying implies necessity or fate, holds that free will stands and that the wording proves it, since he says not they see not but seeing they see not, and observes that the disciples saw what righteous men of old desired and never saw, which joins the two Testaments.

Augustine tries to hold both sides, that they shut their own eyes and so caused God to shut them, but admits that the therefore they could not believe of the fourth Gospel presses hard, and concludes they had deserved it by earlier sins.

debates.question: Is the blindness of the hearers chosen or imposed?

Imposed, Christ speaking so as to be a riddle and keeping his secrets from the reprobate
Both, since they shut their own eyes, though an earlier desert must be confessed
Penal in purpose, as Mark and Luke show, yet with mercy under the penalty

A secret kept from others and revealed to the initiated

18.pericope_label: Hear ye therefore the parable of the sower. When any one heareth the word of the kingdom, and understandeth it not, then cometh the wicked one, and catcheth away that which was sown in his heart. This is he which received seed by the way side. But he that received the seed into stony places, the same is he that heareth the word, and anon with joy receiveth it; Yet hath he not root in himself, but dureth for a while: for when tribulation or persecution ariseth because of the word, by and by he is offended. He also that received seed among the thorns is he that heareth the word; and the care of this world, and the deceitfulness of riches, choke the word, and he becometh unfruitful. But he that received seed into the good ground is he that heareth the word, and understandeth it; which also beareth fruit, and bringeth forth, some an hundredfold, some sixty, some thirty.

schools.summary: Ellicott and Robertson both note that the ye is emphatic, what is withheld from others being given to these. Ellicott traces the sequence in the first hearer, who hears, fails to take it in, the fault being moral rather than intellectual, and has the word lifted out of his memory; he answers the oddity of many birds standing for one tempter by saying that whatever makes men forget the truth does the enemy's work, and on the stony ground presses the point on method, that the more a system works by excitement the oftener such results appear. Robertson notes that Matthew speaks of the hearers as themselves the seed, locates the blame not in the seed but in the man who lets it be snatched, has the devil snatching like a bandit before the grain can sprout, and calls the second hearer a mushroom growth, quick to sprout and quick to stumble, a picture of some converts in modern revivals. Barnes takes Mark's how then will ye know all parables as a sign that this is among the simplest, says the gospel preached to hardened men lies like seed on the beaten path, and describes the second hearer as caught by the gospel as by something new.

Calvin sets out the four kinds and then guards against arithmetic, since Christ fixed no number and the produce of faith is not always alike; his sharpest point is who is left out, for no open despiser appears here, only men with some appearance of docility, so that if the greater part even of these perish the case of the rest grows dark. Gill hears in Mark's added question a reproof for dulness in men who had received grace, and insists that the second hearer is not careless like the first but settled and diligent.

Clarke observes that the three evangelists use three names for the enemy, the tormentor, the adversary who opposes every purpose of amendment, and the one whose name means to dart through, and makes the careless heart an open road where evil affections pass unchecked, the devil's thoroughfare; on the stony ground he speaks of fallow never ploughed and a man who never felt his own sore. Wesley divides the theft between inward thoughts and outward agents who raise other subjects, allows the joy of the second hearer to be real, even transport, and then finds no change in the ground of the heart; he distributes the thorns, cares to the poor, wealth to the rich, the desire of other things to all.

Augustine offers orders of life for the three yields, a hundredfold for martyrs, sixtyfold for virgins, thirtyfold for the married, or else three degrees in which death is despised; he rejects a reading current in his day that the saints would deliver thirty or sixty or a hundred souls at the judgment, because men were using it to promise themselves impunity.

debates.question: What do the hundred, sixty and thirty stand for?

positions.position: Orders of life, or degrees in which death is despised
Simply various proportions of fruitfulness, not to be pressed

debates.question: Where does the loss of the seed lie?

positions.position: With the man who lets it be snatched, not with the seed
With defects in hearers who are not open despisers but men of some docility
With a heart left open as a thoroughfare

24.pericope_label: Another parable put he forth unto them, saying, The kingdom of heaven is likened unto a man which sowed good seed in his field: But while men slept, his enemy came and sowed tares among the wheat, and went his way. But when the blade was sprung up, and brought forth fruit, then appeared the tares also. So the servants of the householder came and said unto him, Sir, didst not thou sow good seed in thy field? from whence then hath it tares? He said unto them, An enemy hath done this. The servants said unto him, Wilt thou then that we go and gather them up? But he said, Nay; lest while ye gather up the tares, ye root up also the wheat with them. Let both grow together until the harvest: and in the time of harvest I will say to the reapers, Gather ye together first the tares, and bind them in bundles to burn them: but gather the wheat into my barn.

schools.summary: Robertson refuses the word tares and calls it darnel, a bastard wheat common in Palestine, like the true grain except that its seeds are black and indistinguishable until near harvest, and notes that intermingled roots come up together. Ellicott orders the audience, the sower expounded in the boat and the tares, mustard seed and leaven spoken again to the crowd, and reads the refusal to weed as a question of timing, the householder being a pattern of patient wisdom who can defeat the malice but will choose his hour. Barnes takes the field for the world, makes the darkness moral as well as literal, and warns that one of the enemy's arts in a revival is to spread plausible notions of piety until multitudes think themselves Christians who are not. Lightfoot presses the rabbinic point that wheat and this weed are not reckoned seeds of different kinds, so that the whole field was sown with wheat of one sort or the other and the parable distinguishes good Christians from bad rather than good men from bad.

Calvin turns the parable toward the discouraged, holding that its object is not to warn a mixed multitude but to keep the godly from despondency at the sight of good and bad confused, since many under pretence of zeal grow displeased and, finding absolute purity nowhere, withdraw. Gill marks the shift of subject from sorts of hearers to members within churches, and catalogues the sleep of a church at length, grace unexercised, duty done sluggishly, lukewarmness about Christ's cause and unconcern about sins of omission, warning that such churches fill with hypocrites and heretics.

Clarke hunts the term through the rabbinic writers, where it means grain that was right seed at first and afterwards degenerated, adds from an old agricultural handbook that darnel baked into bread dims the eyes, and lays the sleep at the door of lukewarm professors and indolent pastors. Wesley reads the kingdom of heaven here as the gospel dispensation, warns that is like means only that the thing may be illustrated, answers the sleep in a line, that they ought to have watched for the Lord of the field sleepeth not, makes the darnel the outside Christian who has the form without the power, and finds in an enemy hath done this a plain reply to the question of the origin of evil.
Henry declines to separate the parable from its exposition, since each explains the other.

Chrysostom orders the matter historically, that error came after truth, false prophets after prophets and Antichrist after Christ, since the devil attempts nothing unless he sees something to imitate; and he takes the refusal to weed as a standing prohibition of putting heretics to death, which would bring a war without end into the world.

Augustine takes the sleep of the heads of the Church and the sleep of death of the apostles, and asks whether heretics are meant or Catholics of evil life, deciding for heretics since the field is the world and not the Church, while men who live badly in the same faith are better called chaff, which shares stem and root with the grain.

debates.question: Who are the tares?

positions.position: Heretics rather than Catholics of evil life, the merely immoral being chaff and not tares
Outside Christians with the form of godliness and not the power
Bad Christians as distinct from bad men, the whole field being sown with wheat of one kind or another

debates.question: What does the refusal to root them up forbid?

positions.position: The killing of heretics, which would bring endless war into the world
Only prematurity, since the householder means to act at the right time
Nothing beyond the practical difficulty of intermingled roots

debates.question: What is the object of the parable?

positions.position: To keep the godly from despondency at the mixture, not to warn a mixed multitude
To show the difference of members within churches

31.pericope_label: Another parable put he forth unto them, saying, The kingdom of heaven is like to a grain of mustard seed, which a man took, and sowed in his field: Which indeed is the least of all seeds: but when it is grown, it is the greatest among herbs, and becometh a tree, so that the birds of the air come and lodge in the branches thereof. Another parable spake he unto them; The kingdom of heaven is like unto leaven, which a woman took, and hid in three measures of meal, till the whole was leavened. All these things spake Jesus unto the multitude in parables; and without a parable spake he not unto them: That it might be fulfilled which was spoken by the prophet, saying, I will open my mouth in parables; I will utter things which have been kept secret from the foundation of the world.

schools.summary: Ellicott takes the two parables as left unexplained on purpose, to train the disciples in interpreting, observes that what we call mustard grows into nothing that could be called a tree and that the least of all seeds is popular description not to be pressed with microscopic exactness, and makes the seed here not the word but the Christian society itself, smaller at sowing than any sect in Palestine and destined to outgrow every kingdom; he notes that the birds have changed sides since the first parable and now stand for the institutions that shelter under it. Robertson agrees that it is a tree not in nature but in size, an excusable exaggeration in popular speech, says the leaven stands for pervasive power and refuses the objection that leaven means corruption as exegetical jugglery, since the devil is called a lion and so is Christ, and adds that three measures is simply a common baking and that finding the Trinity in it is beside the mark. Barnes explains the plant by climate and kind, since it took years to become a tree where ours is an annual herb, allows both scales of the parable, and cautions that young converts suppose they have much religion when they are like a blind man just restored to sight. Lightfoot brings the Talmud in evidence, the mustard stalk at Sichin and the proverb that makes a grain of mustard the measure of the smallest thing, and measures three sata against an ephah.

Calvin puts the parable to pastoral use, that profane men despise the gospel because its ministers are of slender reputation and its converts of no consideration, and that the Lord opened his reign with a despicable beginning on purpose, that his power might be better known by a progress nobody expected. Gill says the first parable showed the state of the church to the end and this its small beginnings and large increase.

Clarke brings the same Talmudic evidence as Lightfoot, the stalk whose broken bough roofed a potter's tent and the rabbi who climbed into the one in his field, and takes the inward scale as well, that grace often begins in a single good desire. Wesley marks the change of subject, that the earlier parables concerned unfruitful hearers and these those who bear fruit, reduces the superlative to idiom, one of the least, and calls the three measures the usual baking.

Henry states the scope, that the beginnings would be small and the latter end great, and describes the working of the leaven as certain, gradual and silent, the apostles hiding a handful of it in the mass of mankind.

Chrysostom keeps to the working of the leaven, that as it changes much flour into its own kind so shall the disciples change the world, and notes that the word is hid rather than put, so that when they are cast down by enemies they shall overcome them; on the closing citation he says the Evangelist quotes the prophet so nobody should think the method new.

Augustine makes the leaven love because it causes fermentation, the woman wisdom, and the three measures either heart and soul and mind, or the three degrees of fruitfulness, or Noah and Daniel and Job; on the closing verse he narrows the claim, that he spake nothing without a parable does not mean he never used plain words but that no discourse closed without one somewhere in it.

36.pericope_label: Then Jesus sent the multitude away, and went into the house: and his disciples came unto him, saying, Declare unto us the parable of the tares of the field. He answered and said unto them, He that soweth the good seed is the Son of man; The field is the world; the good seed are the children of the kingdom; but the tares are the children of the wicked one; The enemy that sowed them is the devil; the harvest is the end of the world; and the reapers are the angels. As therefore the tares are gathered and burned in the fire; so shall it be in the end of this world. The Son of man shall send forth his angels, and they shall gather out of his kingdom all things that offend, and them which do iniquity; And shall cast them into a furnace of fire: there shall be wailing and gnashing of teeth. Then shall the righteous shine forth as the sun in the kingdom of their Father. Who hath ears to hear, let him hear.

schools.summary: Robertson is emphatic that the article stands with both nouns, so that field and world are coextensive, and that both the good seed and the darnel are sown in the world and not in the kingdom or the church, gathering out of his kingdom meaning out from the midst, since good and bad lie scattered together in every city. Ellicott places the question in Peter's house, infers that the disciples found this parable harder than the other two, holds that it is about the new order called the Church and explains the evil found in it, touching the wider world only by inference, and rejects the identification of the tares with heretics, since the passage defines them as all things that offend and them which do iniquity. Barnes refuses to settle whether the furnace means material fire, insisting only that Christ would not hold out frightful images merely to terrify.

Calvin guards both ends of the answer about the enemy, that when wicked men are mingled with believers this is neither accident nor nature but the devil's trick, and that saying so acquits God and not the men; he admits how distressing it is that the Church is burdened with the reprobate to the end, and holds both halves, that patience is enjoined and that pastors must still labour to purify it. Gill treats hypocrites and heretics in churches as proof of that enmity, and takes the field for the whole world or the church in its several parts.

Clarke says that after a thousand volumes on the origin of evil we shall know exactly what Christ says here, that an enemy hath done it, since God could not produce sin, nothing producing what is not in itself, and describes the enemy as deceitful, vigilant while men sleep, and hidden once he has sown; he draws the moral that men who attend only the public preaching will not understand the mysteries, which are learned by secret prayer. Wesley notes that the Greek behind the phrase is simply all scandals, whatever hindered the seed from rooting.

Chrysostom notes that he had spoken in parables to draw questions and got none, that no scribe followed him indoors, which shows they had followed only to catch him, and that the disciples now ask freely, passing over the leaven and the mustard seed as plain; he observes that the figure of harvest is used in two senses, since elsewhere the fields are already white and one sows while another reaps, whereas here the same sows and reaps and the harvest is the end, and concludes from the sowing of his own field that this world is his.

Origen reads the withdrawal both ways, that when Jesus is with the multitudes he is not in his house, and that it springs from his love of men to leave the house for those who cannot come to him; on the field he says the whole world might be called a field, and not the Church.
Augustine finds it fitting that angels separate, since the good can discharge punishment with a good spirit as a judge does, while the wicked cannot perform offices of mercy.

44.pericope_label: Again, the kingdom of heaven is like unto treasure hid in a field; the which when a man hath found, he hideth, and for joy thereof goeth and selleth all that he hath, and buyeth that field. Again, the kingdom of heaven is like unto a merchant man, seeking goodly pearls: Who, when he had found one pearl of great price, went and sold all that he had, and bought it.

schools.summary: Ellicott keeps the buried hoard rather than a mine and sets it in village life, where tales ran of men made suddenly rich by treasure concealed in war, and answers the moral difficulty by saying that parables do not concern themselves with such questions, any more than those of the unjust steward and the unjust judge, Jewish casuistry having laid the rule of caution on the seller. Barnes says plainly the conduct would be dishonest and integrity required the finder to tell the owner, but adds that Christ does not vindicate it and only describes how men actually get wealth, the point lying in the earnestness. Robertson thinks the morality need not be bad at all, since a man might hide a find to keep it from thieves, and says it is not the point in any case.

Calvin says both parables are meant to make believers prefer this to the whole world, since we are so captivated by its allurements that eternal life fades from view, and that treasure is the apt figure because its worth is undiminished though buried out of sight. Gill inverts the parable of the pearl, making Christ the merchant who sought and purchased his elect, who are to him the pearl of great price.

Clarke refuses a buried pot and argues for a mine, since there is no sense in buying a field for money a man might carry off as readily and as honestly; on his reading hid means kept secret until the purchase, and the gospel is a mine whose veins run everywhere through the Scriptures, so the field must be dug. Wesley agrees that these are proposed peculiarly to the apostles and makes the kingdom within a treasure hidden from the world and from the wisest in it, which a man having found hides deep in his heart.

Henry divides the figure, Christ the treasure and the gospel the field, hid as milk in the breast, marrow in the bone, honey in the comb, and hid not in an enclosed garden but in an open field where anyone may dig; he finds there the reason so many slight it, that they look only at the surface of the field.

Chrysostom marks the change of theme, that the leaven and the mustard seed showed the power of the preaching and these two its value, and keeps the pearl with the preaching, since two things are required of a preacher, detachment and watchfulness, and truth being one there is one pearl; a man carrying a pearl knows his wealth while others do not, since it hides in the hand for its smallness.

Origen asks whether these are parables at all, since Scripture attaches the word elsewhere and withholds it here, and presses the wording of the pearl, that the merchant sold not merely the pearls he had bought but everything he had, before turning aside into the natural history of pearls, those of the land and the better sort out of the sea.

Augustine offers Christ, the one man without sin, or love of the neighbour, in which the Apostle says all is comprehended, or the Word in which all things are contained, and concludes that whatever the pearl is, its price is the possession of ourselves, since we can give nothing more. Gregory makes it the sweetness of the heavenly kingdom, which a man having tasted leaves willingly what he loved before.

Christ, or love of the neighbour, or the Word, and in any case the possession of ourselves

47.pericope_label: Again, the kingdom of heaven is like unto a net, that was cast into the sea, and gathered of every kind: Which, when it was full, they drew to shore, and sat down, and gathered the good into vessels, but cast the bad away. So shall it be at the end of the world: the angels shall come forth, and sever the wicked from among the just, And shall cast them into the furnace of fire: there shall be wailing and gnashing of teeth. Jesus saith unto them, Have ye understood all these things? They say unto him, Yea, Lord. Then said he unto them, Therefore every scribe which is instructed unto the kingdom of heaven is like unto a man that is an householder, which bringeth forth out of his treasure things new and old.

schools.summary: Ellicott distinguishes the great drag-net from the hand-net of the earlier chapter and closes the day of parables on a lesson the fishermen could read at sight; he names the same two thoughts as in the tares, the mingling and the separation, but points at what the parable leaves out, that the casting of the net is meant to change what it catches, so that those who remain bad are bad by their own will, and notes that the verb in the closing question is the one used of the sower's hearers. Robertson gives the word that became seine, notes that as the field was the world so this net takes every fish in the sea, adds Homer's picture of the slain suitors lying like fish in nets of myriad meshes, and keeps the householder as a character sketch, the merely rabbinical scribe producing only the old and stale while the disciple of the kingdom stays fresh-minded. Barnes says the parable does not differ in meaning from the tares, hears the kindness in the closing question, and ends on the duty, that the store is not to lie unemployed. Lightfoot dissolves the difficulty of things new and old into idiom, since the schools debated whether new or old produce should be used in holy things and a provident man kept both by him.

Calvin takes both readings of the parable, that the Church while it lasts is a mixture and that the disciples are warned off the empty title of faith, since it is of little consequence to be gathered into the fold unless we are his own sheep. Gill notes that the gospel is mean in the world's esteem, and that a net does nothing unless cast, nor then unless the blessing follows.

Clarke assigns the parts of the figure, the net the preaching, the sea the abyss of sin from which men are drawn, the hauling ashore the end of all things. Wesley ends on the duty with Barnes, that a prepared preacher holds a store out of which every sort of instruction can be brought.

Chrysostom finds the difference from the tares in the ground of ruin, since there men are lost by evil dogma, in the sower by inattention, and here by an evil life, so that men drawn in the net and knowing God may still not be saved; the parable is added so that we should not think faith alone enough, and he notes that Christ praised the disciples for understanding.

Origen interrupts with a caution about the whole method, that likenesses are never likenesses in every respect, a painting in wax keeping surface and colour but not the hollows and a statue the hollows and not the colour, so that when the kingdom is likened to a thing the comparison holds only where it is required; he then turns the figure on the Scriptures, the net being of variegated texture like the Old and the New woven of thoughts of every kind.

Augustine observes that he said not old and new, preferring the order of value to that of time, and turns it against the Manichaeans, who by keeping only the new promises remain in the old man of the flesh, taking the two as the Testaments. Gregory objects directly to that reading: if the Testaments are meant we must deny that Abraham was learned, who knew the deeds without the words, and refuse Moses the name of householder, who composed one Testament without the words of the other; he also makes the net the Church, given into the hands of fishers, gathering wise and foolish, free and slave.

debates.question: What are the things new and old?

positions.position: The two Testaments, value taking precedence of time, against the Manichaeans
Not the Testaments, since Abraham and Moses would then be unlearned, but men of the later Church

The freshness of the disciple set against the staleness of the rabbinic scribe

It adds a warning against resting in the mere profession of faith
The same two thoughts, with the unstated point that the net is meant to change the fish

53.pericope_label: And it came to pass, that when Jesus had finished these parables, he departed thence. And when he was come into his own country, he taught them in their synagogue, insomuch that they were astonished, and said, Whence hath this man this wisdom, and these mighty works? Is not this the carpenter’s son? is not his mother called Mary? and his brethren, James, and Joses, and Simon, and Judas? And his sisters, are they not all with us? Whence then hath this man all these things? And they were offended in him. But Jesus said unto them, A prophet is not without honour, save in his own country, and in his own house. And he did not many mighty works there because of their unbelief.

schools.summary: Ellicott admits a dislocation however the accounts are arranged and concedes the near absence of trustworthy notes of sequence, but declines to identify this visit with the one in Luke, since that is set at the very beginning and reports violence where here there is only amazement. Barnes adds from Mark that it was a Sabbath, any Jew called on by the minister having the right to address the people, and takes Mark's blunter the carpenter as near proof that Jesus worked at the trade till thirty. Robertson puts the puzzle plainly, that people are often baffled how a boy they knew became the man he seems, takes the brethren for younger half brothers and sisters, and has their disbelief blocking the power to work cures.

Calvin agrees that the narratives are nearly similar and not the same, finds in the second rejection proof that the interval had reformed nobody, and says they ought to have seen the hand of God in a teacher who had not learned letters, while ingratitude dazzled them instead. Gill weighs the word for the trade, which covers any craftsman, reports Epiphanius making the sisters Joseph's daughters by an earlier wife, and tells of the schoolmaster at Antioch who, asked in mockery what the carpenter's son was doing, answered that he was making a coffin for Julian.

Clarke notes that the townsmen appear to have heard none of his doctrine until now and draws the rule that those who should know Christ best are often most ignorant of him; he reports the old Latin copies that read the son of Joseph the carpenter, thinks our Lord worked at the trade through the thirty years, and though allowing that Hebrew usage can stretch brethren to near relations, doubts it, asking why another family's children should share a reproach aimed at one household. Wesley makes the brethren kinsmen, sons of Mary the wife of Cleophas, and turns the closing verse on his own readers, that mighty works are scarce now not because faith is unplanted but because unbelief prevails.

Henry marks the persistence, that his countrymen had rejected him once and he came again, since Christ does not take refusers at their first word, quotes Seneca that a man loves his country not because it is beautiful but because it is his own, and says prejudiced spirits enquire more into a man's rise than into his reasons, turning against him what was really for him.

Chrysostom identifies the country as Nazareth, not Capernaum, observes that here the teaching rather than the miracles causes wonder, answers that illustrious sons came of ignoble fathers, David of a husbandman and Amos of a shepherd, and explains the scarcity of miracles by saying he looked not to display but to profit, working a few so none could plead that none were done.

Origen turns the opening clause against his own earlier argument, that if what was spoken in the house were similitudes and not parables the words when Jesus had finished these parables will not cover them; he reads the townsmen's question as unwilling testimony, since whence hath this man this wisdom concedes a surpassing wisdom.

Augustine notes that the passage from the parables to what follows has no evident connexion, Mark and Luke both going on to a different event, and thinks it no wonder that kinsmen on the mother's side should be called brethren, when men who took him for Joseph's son called others brethren through Joseph.
